rules.concept: lexical base distinguished from inflectional forms
rules.statement: A lexical base is the reference form from which the inflectional paradigm is described; it is distinct from any individual inflectional form even though one or more inflected forms often coincide with the base.
rules.condition: For a variable lexeme, identify its lexical base separately from its attested singular, plural or other inflectional forms; a defective lexeme can have a base for which no corresponding independent form exists, and several forms can coincide with the base.

exceptions.description: Defective lexemes may lack a surface form corresponding to the lexical base; several inflectional forms can also be identical to the lexical base.

contrast.text: The dregs settled at the bottom. [plural-only noun, with a lexical base dreg- not used as a plain singular form]
One sheep escaped through the fence. [singular coincides with the lexical base]
Several sheep escaped through the fence. [plural also coincides with the same lexical base]
A worker greeted the visitors. [the singular matches the lexical base of worker]

rules.concept: inflection of simple and complex lexical bases
rules.statement: In English, a lexeme's base can be internally simple or morphologically complex, and regular inflectional operations generally apply to either kind without changing their basic formation rules.
rules.condition: When a noun's lexical base is simple (e.g., dog) or consists of morphological units (e.g., worker), apply the ordinary plural suffixation operation to the complete lexical base, rather than treating internal derivational complexity as a reason for a different plural rule.

contrast.text: Two dogs waited outside the office. [simple base dog, regular plural]
Two workers waited outside the office. [complex base worker, regular plural]
The trainer hired three workers. [inflection attaches to the whole complex lexical base]

rules.statement: English inflection can use suffixation, change to a lexical base such as vowel alternation, or a combination of a suffix and a modified base.
rules.condition: When describing the formation of a noun or verb inflectional form, distinguish a suffix added to an unchanged base from internal vowel replacement and from the combined use of suffixation and a modified base.

contrast.text: Several workers arrived for the shift. [plural formed by -s suffixation]
The dentist examined the patient's teeth. [plural uses a base-internal vowel change]
The bell rang at daybreak. [preterite uses a base-internal vowel change]
The drawer contained six knives. [plural suffix accompanies a changed base-final consonant]

rules.concept: multi-step inflection from an already inflected form
rules.statement: Most English inflectional forms coincide with or are formed directly from the lexical base, but some forms are produced by an additional operation on another inflectional form.
rules.condition: When analysing the genitive plural of a noun such as child, attach the genitive suffix to its plural rather than to the singular base; for the small set of past participles exemplified by trodden, identify the preterite trod as the input to a further -en suffixation.

exceptions.description: The multi-step pattern applies to genitive plurals and only a small subset of past participles, rather than to all inflected forms.

contrast.text: The children's shoes were lined up outside. [genitive plural: child → children → children's]
The child's shoes were lined up outside. [genitive singular contrasted with the plural input]
The old path had been trodden by many travellers. [tread → trod → trodden]
The travellers trod the path at sunrise. [the preterite provides the input for trodden]

rules.statement: Morphological alternation occurs when the same morphological unit has different surface realisations depending on its context, such as the written plural suffix variants -s and -es.
rules.condition: When comparing inflectional forms that encode the same category, identify contextual differences in the realisation of the morphological unit, rather than assigning separate grammatical categories to regular written suffix variants.

contrast.text: The cats rested near the gate. [written plural suffix -s]
The boxes stood by the gate. [written plural suffix -es]
Two foxes crossed the garden. [written plural suffix -es in the same category]
Two birds crossed the garden. [written plural suffix -s in the same category]

rules.statement: An inflectional form is regular if its formation follows a lexeme-independent general rule, but irregular if the lexeme requires specific stored information about that form or one of its components.
rules.condition: When classifying plural, preterite or participial forms, check whether their formation follows productive formation rules without lexical exceptions; where the resulting form must be separately specified for a particular lexeme, classify it as irregular even if it also contains an ordinary affix.

contrast.text: The painter opened two crates. [regular plural formed by general suffixation]
The guests talked until dusk. [regular preterite]
Several children visited the workshop. [lexeme-specific irregular plural]
The shopkeeper bought fresh bread. [irregular preterite]
She knitted a scarf for her friend. [regular spelling change by consonant doubling]

rules.concept: lexeme-specific base alternants within irregular inflection
rules.statement: An inflectional form may be irregular because a lexeme selects a special modified version of its base, even when the suffix itself follows a productive general rule.
rules.condition: For plural nouns such as thief with a voiced base-final consonant in the plural, distinguish ordinary suffixation from the lexeme-specific change in the base; comparison with a lexeme such as chief that lacks this change shows why the whole formation is irregular.

exceptions.description: A base-final f is not generally voiced in plural formation; lexeme-specific nouns such as chief and proof keep the usual consonant.

contrast.text: The guards caught two thieves. [thief has a lexeme-specific voiced plural base alternant plus regular plural suffix]
Three chiefs met in the council room. [chief does not share that irregular consonant change]
The farmer checked the horses' hooves. [hoof has a specialised plural base in the source]
The inspector compared two proofs. [proof retains the ordinary base-final consonant]

rules.statement: Syncretism is identity of pronunciation or spelling between two or more distinct inflectional forms of the same lexeme.
rules.condition: For one lexeme whose paradigm distinguishes grammatical categories such as singular and plural, classify identically pronounced or written forms in those different paradigm cells as syncretic, not as evidence that only one grammatical number exists.

contrast.text: One sheep was resting beneath the tree. [plain singular sheep]
Five sheep were resting beneath the tree. [plain plural sheep, same pronunciation and spelling]
That sheep is marked with blue paint. [singular agreement despite unchanged noun form]
Those sheep are marked with blue paint. [plural agreement despite unchanged noun form]
